newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia's new trio-presidency to rule by consensus.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia's new trio-presidency to rule by consensus.

text.p: Bosnia's newly-elected three- member collective presidency is supposed to set foreign policy for the post-war union and represent the country's Moslem, Serb and Croat communities.
The Bosnian union presidency is comprised of a Moslem, Serb and Croat elected directly from the Serb republic and the Moslem-Croat federation.
The first term of the presidency members will last two years and subsequent terms will last four years under the constitution contained in the Dayton peace treaty.
The candidate with the most votes serves as the president or chairman of the presidency for two years.
The three members are obliged to take decisions by consensus. A similar arrangement created political gridlock in old Yugoslavia but diplomats say it is the only way to accommodate rival factions.

Before war erupted in the spring of 1992, Serb members of the country's old collective presidency had already walked out to protest plans by Moslem and Croat parties to break from Serbian-led Yugoslavia.
In the event a consensus cannot be reached, the country's constitution allows for two of the three members to take a decision.

The third member has the right to declare the decision as damaging the vital interest of his community and the issue is then referred to the National Assembly of the Serb republic or the House of the People in the Moslem-Croat Federation.
If the objection is upheld by a two-thirds vote in either legislature, the presidency's decision is overturned.
The presidency will appoint a council of ministers, including a foreign minister and trade minister. The appointments must be approved by the Bosnian union House of Representatives.
International mediators have yet to announce where the presidency will meet.
During Sarajevo's siege, the presidency building that housed the offices of President Alija Izetbegovic came under repeated artillery, mortar and sniper fire.
In the fall of 1994, a rocket hit the presidency while U.N. special envoy Yasushi Akashi was holding talks with Izetbegovic.
